passage:
"He said he just wasn't feeling it any more. What does that even mean?" Vasudha's voice cracked.

"I don't know," Parul said, and put the kettle down. "It's a rubbish thing to say."

"I keep going over the last month. Was it my laugh? The way I hugged too long?"

"Vasu."

"I've drafted six messages. I could say I'll change. I could just ask for one more talk."

Parul held out her hand for the phone, and Vasudha, after a moment, gave it up.

"Cry. It's allowed. You're not going to find the perfect reason tonight."

"I feel worthless," Vasudha said. "And stupid, for feeling worthless."

"Then be worthless and stupid on my sofa. I've got biryani and a terrible film." 

Vasudha laughed, wet-eyed. Then she cried again, properly.

qa.q: How many messages had Vasudha drafted?
What might Vasudha be feeling as she goes over the last month, asking about her laugh and her hugs?
qa.a: She is confused and doubting her worth, searching for a reason she did something wrong that would explain the ending.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped Vasudha on that evening?
qa.a: She took the phone so Vasudha would not send a begging message, told her crying is allowed, and offered company and food.

qa.q: How might Parul see the moment when Vasudha hands over the phone?
qa.a: Parul probably feels protective and a bit anxious, wanting to keep her friend from a message she would regret, while staying kind.

grounding: Shows being dumped with worthlessness and confusion, met by open grief, a friend's company and no search for a perfect reason.

passage: When Chaitanya ended things last March, on a Wednesday, in a café near college, I thought I would never feel normal again. I'm Farida, and I spent the next two weeks trying to find the reason. Was it my laugh? My exams? The fight about his cousin's wedding? I made lists. I reread two years of messages at 3 a.m., looking for the moment it went wrong. I drafted long texts begging for one more chance, and deleted them, thank God. I felt worthless, as if someone had officially declared me not enough. What helped wasn't finding the reason. There wasn't one perfect reason; he'd said he just didn't feel it any more. What helped was my friends Salma and Neetu sleeping over three nights in a row, letting me cry and eat terrible pizza and cry again. Somewhere in there, I stopped searching and just grieved. By June I laughed properly for the first time. I still don't know exactly why. I don't need to.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say was the reason?
qa.a: He just didn't feel it any more.

qa.q: How did Farida feel in the weeks after the break-up?
qa.a: Farida felt worthless and confused, as if officially declared not enough.

qa.q: What helped Farida more than searching for a reason?
qa.a: Grieving openly and leaning on Salma and Neetu, who stayed over three nights in a row.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt ending things?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable but honest, saying he no longer felt it rather than inventing a reason.

grounding: A first-person account of being dumped, feeling worthless and confused, and healing by grieving with friends instead of begging or searching for a perfect reason.

passage: Warden's note, boys' hostel, Friday. Dhruv (third year) has been missing meals since Damini ended their relationship last week. Tonight the girls' hostel security told me he had waited at their gate for two hours, asking to see her. When I spoke with him in the common room, he broke down. He said he needed to know exactly why she left, and that he had sent her many messages begging for another chance. He admitted he had thought about posting their old photos 'so she'd feel it too'. I told him the pain was real and understandable, but that waiting at her gate and acting on those thoughts would only hurt both of them and could frighten her. He agreed to stop contacting her and deleted the draft post in front of me. I called his roommate to sit with him tonight, informed the student counsellor, and booked him an appointment for Monday morning.

qa.q: How long did Dhruv wait at the girls' hostel gate?
What was Dhruv feeling when the warden spoke with him?
qa.a: He was heartbroken and desperate, breaking down and needing to know why she left.

qa.q: What steps were taken to help Dhruv?
qa.a: He agreed to stop contacting Damini and deleted the draft post, his roommate sat with him, and a counsellor appointment was booked.

qa.q: How might Damini feel with Dhruv waiting at her gate?
qa.a: Likely uneasy or frightened, since she had ended things and he kept pushing.

grounding: A warden's note on a young man dumped and desperate, turned away from begging, waiting at her gate and revenge, towards grief and support.
